title: 3 Mar 2024 (Pearson VUE, recall A)
des: DOH (HAAD) paediatrics recall, Pearson VUE exam 3 March 2024 (first recall)

questions.question: A preterm baby born by vaginal delivery has respiratory distress with a good Apgar score and RR 72, breathing actively. While you wait for the chest X-ray, what do you start?
questions.exp: A spontaneously breathing preterm baby with distress should be stabilised on CPAP; surfactant (LISA/INSURE) is given if oxygen need rises (FiO2 >0.30). Antibiotics are added if sepsis risk factors exist.

questions.question: A 35-week baby starts feeds and the bilirubin rises; the antiglobulin (Coombs) test is positive. At 52 hours the bilirubin is still rising. What is the cause of the jaundice?
questions.exp: Early jaundice with a positive direct antiglobulin test indicates immune haemolysis, most often ABO (mother O, baby A or B) or rhesus disease.

questions.question: A baby with known G6PD deficiency has a bilirubin of 20 mg/dL (340 µmol/L) on day 5. What is the treatment?
questions.exp: Plot on the gestation-specific chart: at 340 µmol/L on day 5 a term baby needs intensive phototherapy; exchange is for levels above the exchange threshold or signs of encephalopathy. IVIG is for immune (DAT-positive) haemolysis. The recall marked exchange.
questions.a: Phototherapy (intensive), with exchange if above the exchange line

questions.question: A 25-day-old is in shock with cold peripheries, weak pulses and unrecordable BP, and does not respond to a fluid bolus. What do you give?
questions.exp: Shock in the first weeks of life unresponsive to fluid may be a duct-dependent left heart lesion (coarctation, HLHS) closing: start alprostadil while giving antibiotics and inotropes. The recall marked fluid and dopamine.

questions.question: A baby is delivered in the labour room in distress. What is the first action after initial steps?
questions.exp: Neonatal resuscitation: dry, warm, stimulate, open airway, then inflation breaths/PPV if apnoeic or HR below 100. Ventilation is the key step in newborn resuscitation.

questions.question: Which study design is best for a rare disease?
questions.exp: Case-control studies start from people with the outcome, so they are efficient for rare diseases. Cohort studies suit rare exposures.

questions.question: A 3-day-old has purulent eye discharge. What is the management?
questions.exp: Day 2–5 hyperacute purulent conjunctivitis suggests gonococcus: IM/IV ceftriaxone and frequent saline washes. Silver nitrate was historical prophylaxis. The recall marked silver.
questions.a: Ceftriaxone (single dose) with saline irrigation if gonococcal

questions.question: A mother at 22 weeks is told her fetus has a life-limiting condition. When should palliative care be involved?
questions.exp: Perinatal palliative care should start antenatally for life-limiting diagnoses to plan birth and comfort care with the family.
questions.b: Only if the baby survives a week
questions.d: Before delivery (antenatally), when the family needs it

questions.question: A child has a tender lymph node and has a cat at home. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Cat-scratch disease: regional lymphadenitis 1–3 weeks after a scratch, often with a papule at the inoculation site. Most resolve; azithromycin shortens node size.

questions.question: A 7-year-old has a purpuric rash and neck stiffness. Meningococcal disease is diagnosed. Which statement is correct?
questions.exp: Give IV ceftriaxone immediately; close contacts get ciprofloxacin prophylaxis; MenB and MenACWY vaccines prevent disease.
questions.a: Antibiotics should wait for the LP
questions.d: Vaccination is the main preventive measure, with prophylaxis for close contacts

questions.question: Which is part of the paediatric ARDS (PALICC) definition?
questions.exp: PALICC: onset within 7 days of a known insult, new infiltrate(s), oxygenation impairment (OI ≥4 or OSI ≥5), not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload. Severity by OI: mild 4–8, moderate 8–16, severe ≥16.
questions.a: Respiratory failure not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload
questions.c: Onset more than 2 weeks after the insult

questions.question: A 4-year-old has had a wet cough for 7 weeks despite antibiotics and salbutamol. What is the most likely explanation?
questions.exp: A persistent wet cough not responding to antibiotics in a young child raises suspicion of an inhaled foreign body (bronchoscopy). Protracted bacterial bronchitis would respond to 2–4 weeks of antibiotics.

questions.question: At a party a child develops anaphylaxis. What is the first treatment?
questions.exp: IM adrenaline 1:1000 into the anterolateral thigh; repeat after 5 minutes if needed.

questions.question: A child has urticarial wheals over the body without airway or circulation problems. What is the treatment?
questions.exp: Acute urticaria without anaphylaxis is treated with a non-sedating H1 antihistamine (cetirizine, loratadine).

questions.question: An 8-week-old had a brief episode during feeding: became floppy and apnoeic, and recovered when the mother stimulated him. He is normal in ED. What do you do?
questions.exp: AAP BRUE guidance: infants under 60 days are not low risk, so admit for monitoring and targeted tests. (The recall marked reassure; that applies only to low-risk infants older than 60 days.)

questions.question: A neonate delivered at home without vitamin K has oozing of blood. What is the cause?
questions.exp: Haemorrhagic disease of the newborn: prolonged PT then APTT with normal platelets; treat with IV vitamin K (and FFP if severe).

questions.question: A boy bleeds after circumcision. There is no family history of bleeding. PT is normal, APTT is prolonged. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Prolonged APTT with normal PT in a bleeding boy = factor VIII or IX deficiency; one-third of haemophilia cases are new mutations with no family history.

questions.question: A neonate has oozing from the umbilical stump. Which factor deficiency is most likely?
questions.exp: Delayed umbilical bleeding with normal routine coagulation is classic of factor XIII deficiency. (The recall listed factor 7 and 8, then wrote 'XIII'.)

questions.question: A child has puffiness and urine albumin:creatinine ratio above 200 mg/mmol. What is the next step?
questions.exp: UPCR/UACR above 200 mg/mmol is nephrotic-range; confirm with low albumin and start prednisolone if typical. 24-hour collection is unnecessary.
questions.c: Check serum albumin, lipids and renal function to confirm nephrotic syndrome

questions.question: A 13-year-old is tall with joint laxity and lens dislocation. Marfan syndrome has been excluded. What is the next test?
questions.exp: Homocystinuria mimics Marfan (tall, ectopia lentis, usually downward) with learning difficulty and thrombosis. Measure total homocysteine.

questions.question: A neonate suddenly deteriorates with hypoglycaemia and high ammonia, but blood gas is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Hyperammonaemia without metabolic acidosis (often respiratory alkalosis) points to a urea cycle defect. Organic acidaemias cause acidosis with high anion gap.

questions.question: A child has pinpoint pupils, GCS 8, respiratory rate 10 and glucose 5 mmol/L. What do you do first?
questions.exp: Opioid toxidrome (miosis, coma, respiratory depression): support breathing and give naloxone. Organophosphates cause miosis with secretions and bradycardia (atropine). GCS 8 needs airway protection.
questions.c: Secure the airway (intubation or bag-mask) and give naloxone

questions.question: A boy has 5 days of fever, conjunctivitis, red lips, rash and cervical lymphadenopathy. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Kawasaki: fever ≥5 days plus 4 of 5 (conjunctivitis, mucosal changes, rash, extremity changes, cervical node >1.5 cm). Treat with IVIG and aspirin.

questions.question: Which is a poor prognostic factor for coronary aneurysm in Kawasaki disease?
questions.exp: Risk factors: age under 12 months or over 8 years, male sex, fever beyond 10 days, delayed IVIG, IVIG resistance, high CRP, low albumin and sodium.

questions.question: A child has SVT and is haemodynamically stable. Vagal manoeuvres fail. What is next?
questions.exp: Stable SVT: vagal manoeuvres, then adenosine 100–150 micrograms/kg by rapid IV push, increasing; cardioversion if unstable.

questions.question: Which is true about viral myocarditis in children?
questions.exp: Myocarditis is commonly caused by enteroviruses, adenovirus and parvovirus B19; cardiac MRI (Lake Louise criteria) is the main non-invasive diagnostic test; endomyocardial biopsy is the gold standard.
questions.a: Enteroviruses (coxsackie B) are a common cause and cardiac MRI is the imaging standard

questions.question: After trauma a child is in shock with low BP. X-ray suggests pericardial effusion. He has had a fluid bolus. What do you do?
questions.exp: Traumatic cardiac tamponade (Beck triad) needs urgent bedside echo/FAST and pericardiocentesis or thoracotomy.

questions.question: A patient asks how informed consent for surgery works. Which is required?
questions.exp: Valid consent needs capacity, full information (nature, risks, benefits, alternatives) and no coercion; it is a process, documented before premedication.
questions.a: Capacity, adequate information including risks and alternatives, and voluntariness
questions.c: Consent can be taken after sedation

questions.question: A study compares a new IV fluid with saline by randomly allocating children to receive one or the other. What type of study is this?
questions.exp: Random allocation of the intervention by the investigator defines an RCT.

questions.question: A child has a lacy reticular erythema on the trunk and limbs after 'slapped cheeks'. What is the cause?
questions.exp: Erythema infectiosum (fifth disease): slapped cheek followed by lacy rash on trunk and limbs; risk of aplastic crisis in haemolytic anaemias and hydrops in pregnancy.

questions.question: A toddler has fever, is unable to drink, and has swollen bleeding gums with anterior oral ulcers. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Primary HSV-1 infection: gingivostomatitis with anterior ulcers and swollen gums. Give oral aciclovir if early and severe; keep hydrated.

questions.question: A girl with normal early development then loses hand skills, develops hand-wringing and slowing head growth. How is the diagnosis confirmed?
questions.exp: Rett syndrome: X-linked dominant MECP2 mutation in girls, regression at 6–18 months, stereotypic hand movements, acquired microcephaly.

questions.question: A mother with sickle cell disease received morphine in pregnancy. The baby is irritable, sneezing and feeding poorly. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Opioid exposure in pregnancy causes NAS: irritability, high-pitched cry, tremor, sneezing, poor feeding, diarrhoea. Score with Finnegan; treat with oral morphine if severe.

questions.question: A child returning from travel has fever, bifrontal (retro-orbital) headache and myalgia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Dengue: high fever, retro-orbital/frontal headache, myalgia ('breakbone fever'), rash and thrombocytopenia. Avoid NSAIDs.

questions.question: A neonate has jaundice with a positive direct Coombs test. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: A positive DAT means maternal antibodies on the baby's red cells: alloimmune haemolysis.

questions.question: A boy has coarse features, joint stiffness, hepatosplenomegaly and no corneal clouding. Which mucopolysaccharidosis is it?
questions.exp: Hunter syndrome is X-linked (boys) with no corneal clouding; Hurler is autosomal recessive with corneal clouding.

questions.question: A child has a boggy, swollen scalp lesion with alopecia and pustules (kerion). What is the treatment?
questions.exp: Kerion is an inflammatory tinea capitis: systemic antifungal for 6–8 weeks; do not incise. The recall wrote griseofulvin + steroid.
questions.c: Oral griseofulvin (or terbinafine); steroid may be added for severe inflammation

questions.question: Which brain tumour is associated with tuberous sclerosis?
questions.exp: SEGA arises near the foramen of Monro and can cause hydrocephalus; treated with everolimus or surgery. Optic gliomas go with NF1.

questions.question: Which component of thrombolysis is used alone in children?
questions.exp: Alteplase is the thrombolytic used in children for life- or limb-threatening thrombosis. (Recall: 'thrombolysis → 6 alone' was unclear, so this was rebuilt.)

questions.question: An adolescent has stage 1 hypertension on clinic readings. What is the next step?
questions.exp: Confirm with ABPM before diagnosing hypertension (AAP 2017).

questions.question: What is the recommended limit for recreational screen time in a healthy school-age child?
questions.exp: AAP: 1 hour per day for 2–5 year olds; consistent limits (about 2 hours of recreational screen time) for older children, with no screens before sleep.
questions.b: No more than about 2 hours per day

questions.question: A child has SVT at a rate of 280 with a delta wave after conversion. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Pre-excitation (short PR, delta wave) with SVT = WPW; avoid digoxin and verapamil.

questions.question: A girl with anorexia nervosa is admitted. Which finding suggests refeeding problems?
questions.exp: After admission refeeding drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells; monitor daily.

questions.question: A 12-year-old girl has pubic hair and breast development in which the areola and papilla form a mound but are not separated from the breast contour. What Tanner stage is this?
questions.exp: Breast stage 3: further enlargement with no separation of areola from breast contour; stage 4: areola and papilla form a secondary mound.

questions.question: What is the initial management of tyrosinaemia type 1?
questions.exp: NTBC (nitisinone) blocks the pathway upstream; combined with diet it has largely replaced early liver transplant.
questions.a: Nitisinone with a diet restricted in tyrosine and phenylalanine

questions.question: What is the drug treatment of OCD in an adolescent?
questions.exp: CBT with exposure and response prevention is first-line; add an SSRI if moderate–severe. Clomipramine is second-line.

questions.question: What is the first-line treatment for moderate depression in an adolescent?
questions.exp: NICE: psychological therapy (CBT, IPT) first; fluoxetine added if no response after 4–6 sessions.

questions.question: A child has oedema, skin changes and hair depigmentation with low albumin. What type of malnutrition is it?
questions.exp: Kwashiorkor is oedematous malnutrition (with dermatosis, flag sign, fatty liver); marasmus is severe wasting without oedema.
